audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does get_storage_root callback return the correct, canonical 32-byte storage root for each address?
audit_items.state_context: beacon-chain/state/state-native/state_trie.go: SSZ beacon state SSZ Merkle tree using SHA-256. No RLP, no keccak256, no EVM Merkle Patricia Trie, no get_storage_root.

phase1.summary: The property targets get_storage_root callback returning a canonical 32-byte EVM storage root. The resolved code (HashTreeRoot/initializeMerkleLayers in state_trie.go) is the SSZ beacon state Merkle hash tree root computation using SHA-256. No get_storage_root function, no StorageRoot type, and no execution-layer account storage abstraction exists anywhere in this codebase.
state_anomalies_found: get_storage_root function does not exist in the target codebase — no file, no function, no symbol
HashTreeRoot returns a [32]byte SSZ SHA-256 Merkle root of beacon state fields, not an EVM storage trie root
Resolution was performed by grep_fallback on 'trie' in the filename — domain mismatch: SSZ binary Merkle tree vs. EVM Merkle Patricia Trie are entirely different constructs
phase1.cache_analysis: initializeMerkleLayers uses lazy-init: if len(b.merkleLayers) > 0 returns immediately. This cache is for beacon state SSZ root, not EVM storage roots. No storage root caching exists.
phase1.concurrency_analysis: HashTreeRoot acquires b.lock.Lock() (exclusive write lock) for the entire operation. The property's concern about concurrent storage root callbacks is not applicable here.

phase2.summary: No code path exists through which an attacker-controlled input causes get_storage_root to be invoked, because the function does not exist. HashTreeRoot takes only a context.Context input, not attacker-controlled for changing root computation logic.
phase2.counterexample: N/A — function under test does not exist in target codebase
attack_scenarios: No attack scenario applicable: the property's target function is absent from this codebase entirely

phase2_5.summary: Prysm is a consensus client, not an execution client. It does not process EVM transactions or compute EVM storage roots. The execution-layer storage root is a field within ExecutionPayloadHeader that Prysm receives from the execution client — Prysm trusts this value without recomputing it.
entry_points: None within Prysm for EVM storage root computation
phase2_5.attack_surface: No attack surface in Prysm for this property. EVM storage root computed by execution layer client (outside this codebase).

phase3.summary: The invariant 'get_storage_root returns a canonical 32-byte root' cannot be proven or falsified — the function is absent. HashTreeRoot does produce a [32]byte output (enforced by bytesutil.ToBytes32) but this is irrelevant to the property under test.
edge_cases: Property subject function does not exist in target codebase

phase3_5.reason: The property (get_storage_root EVM storage root callback) does not map to any code in the Prysm beacon chain codebase. This is an execution-layer concern and out of scope for a consensus client audit. The code resolution was incorrect (grep_fallback matched 'trie' in filename). No vulnerability finding possible when subject function is absent.
phase3_5.recommendation: Re-target to the execution layer client (e.g., go-ethereum or reth) implementing get_storage_root. If audit scope is Prysm only, mark out-of-scope.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is keccak256 producing consistent, deterministic 32-byte output for all inputs?
audit_items.state_context: keccak256 exists at crypto/hash/hash.go (deposit event signature) and crypto/keystore/keccak256.go (keystore MAC). Not used for EVM trie operations. HashTreeRoot uses SHA-256 not keccak256.

phase1.summary: The property audits keccak256 for determinism and 32-byte output consistency in the context of EVM trie operations. The resolved code (HashTreeRoot) uses SHA-256 for SSZ Merkle operations. keccak256 exists in crypto/hash/hash.go and crypto/keystore/keccak256.go but is not used for storage trie operations. The sync.Pool in hash.go is a standard safe pattern with h.Reset() before use.
state_anomalies_found: Keccak256 in crypto/hash/hash.go uses sync.Pool for hasher reuse — safe pattern with h.Reset() before each operation
The keccak256Pool.Get() call has type assertion with fallback: if !ok { h = sha3.NewLegacyKeccak256() } — correct defensive coding
In crypto/keystore/keccak256.go, a new sha3.NewLegacyKeccak256() is created on every call with no pooling — no state reuse risk
Keccak256 in hash.go calls h.Reset() before use and defers pool return — correct pattern, no state leakage between calls
phase1.cache_analysis: keccak256Pool uses sync.Pool with proper Reset() before each hash operation. Pooled hashers are reset before use, preventing state leakage. This is the correct pattern.
phase1.concurrency_analysis: sync.Pool is goroutine-safe by design. defer keccak256Pool.Put(h) returns the hasher after Sum() is called. No window where a hasher could be used concurrently. No race condition possible in the pool usage pattern.

phase2.summary: Auditing the actual Keccak256 implementation in crypto/hash/hash.go: returns [32]byte (exactly 32 bytes, enforced by Go type system). h.Sum(b[:0]) appends hash to fixed-size array slice, always 32 bytes for keccak256. Function is deterministic: same input always produces same output. sha3.NewLegacyKeccak256() from golang.org/x/crypto/sha3 is a well-tested standard library implementation.
phase2.counterexample: No counterexample found. The implementation correctly produces deterministic 32-byte output.
attack_scenarios: Pool corruption scenario: not possible — sync.Pool is an isolated pool for keccak256 hashers only; no cross-contamination with SHA-256 used in Merkle operations
No practical attack scenario found against the actual keccak256 usage in this codebase
phase2.timing_dependencies: None. keccak256 is a pure deterministic function with no timing-dependent state.

phase2_5.summary: Keccak256 in this codebase is used for: (1) deposit event signature (fixed constant, computed once at package init), (2) keystore MAC computation. Neither use involves attacker-controlled EVM storage keys or addresses. The property's scenario (keccak256 fundamental to trie operations) does not apply.
entry_points: crypto/hash/hash.go:Keccak256 — called from beacon-chain/execution/log_processing.go for deposit event signature (fixed input, not attacker-controlled for hash correctness)
crypto/keystore/keccak256.go:Keccak256 — called from keystore operations for MAC verification
phase2_5.attack_surface: Keccak256 not used for EVM trie operations. Its actual usages are not in the attack surface described by this property.

phase3.summary: The invariant (keccak256 returns deterministic 32-byte output) is provably satisfied for Keccak256 in crypto/hash/hash.go: return type [32]byte enforces exactly 32 bytes at compile time; sha3.NewLegacyKeccak256 is standards-conformant; pool pattern with Reset() prevents state contamination. However, the property's intended scope (keccak256 for EVM trie operations) does not apply to this codebase.
phase3.guard_identified: Go type system enforces [32]byte return; sha3.NewLegacyKeccak256 from golang.org/x/crypto produces standards-conformant keccak256; h.Reset() clears state between pool reuses
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Guards are sufficient for actual keccak256 usages in this codebase. But the property's claimed scope (EVM trie operations) is not present.
edge_cases: Empty input: handled correctly by sha3.NewLegacyKeccak256 (standard empty-input keccak256 hash)
Pool exhaustion under high concurrency: sync.Pool handles by creating new instances — safe behavior

phase3_5.reason: The property's subject (keccak256 for EVM storage trie operations) does not exist in Prysm. The actual Keccak256 implementation is correct and deterministic. The resolved code location (state_trie.go HashTreeRoot) uses SHA-256 not keccak256. No vulnerability finding applicable.
phase3_5.recommendation: For actual Keccak256 usage in this codebase (crypto/hash/hash.go), implementation is correct. No action required. For auditing keccak256 in EVM trie operations, target the execution client.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is keccak256 collision resistance maintained for Ethereum address and storage key hashing?
audit_items.state_context: EVM address and storage key hashing via keccak256 is not performed by Prysm. Prysm receives the EVM world state root as an opaque 32-byte field from the execution client. No EVM MPT implementation exists in this codebase.

phase1.summary: The property audits keccak256 collision resistance in the context of Ethereum address and storage key hashing within the EVM MPT. The resolved code (state_trie.go) does not use keccak256 for address or storage key hashing. The actual Keccak256 usage is limited to deposit event signatures and keystore MACs — neither involves Ethereum address hashing in a trie context.
state_anomalies_found: Keccak256 is not used for Ethereum address or storage key hashing anywhere in this codebase — EVM MPT is not implemented in Prysm

In crypto/keystore/keccak256.go, function returns []byte (not [32]byte) — output is not truncated; callers use it for MAC: mac := Keccak256(derivedKey[16:32], cipherText). No truncation of 32-byte output occurs.
In crypto/hash/hash.go, Keccak256 is called with a fixed ABI-encoded deposit event signature string. No address or storage key data flows through this function.
phase1.cache_analysis: sync.Pool pattern in hash.go is safe (Reset() before use, deferred Put). No state leakage. No collision introduced by caching.
phase1.concurrency_analysis: sync.Pool is concurrency-safe. No shared mutable state between concurrent keccak256 invocations. No race condition possible.

phase2.summary: The property's collision scenario (two different addresses/storage keys producing same keccak256 hash, enabling account state overwrite) requires keccak256 to be used for address-keyed trie lookups. This does not occur in Prysm. Keystore MAC usage: attacker controlling cipherText could attempt second-preimage attack, but mitigated by derived key being secret.
phase2.counterexample: No counterexample for the stated property (EVM trie keccak256 collision) since EVM trie is not implemented here.
attack_scenarios: Keystore MAC: Keccak256(derivedKey[16:32], cipherText) — an attacker knowing derivedKey[16:32] could craft cipherText producing target MAC, but this requires knowledge of the derived key which is secret. Informational observation, not a trie collision vulnerability.
No EVM address/storage key hashing collision scenario possible in this codebase
phase2.timing_dependencies: Keystore MAC comparison: should use constant-time comparison to prevent timing side channels. Informational note only, not a bug bounty finding for this property.

phase2_5.summary: EVM address and storage key hashing via keccak256 is not performed by Prysm. Prysm receives the state root of the EVM world state as an opaque 32-byte field within ExecutionPayloadHeader from the execution client. Prysm does not recompute or validate this value — it trusts the execution client's computation. The trust boundary for EVM trie keccak256 collision resistance lies entirely within the execution client.
entry_points: None in Prysm for EVM address/storage key hashing
phase2_5.attack_surface: No attack surface in Prysm. Execution client concern only. The collision scenario (account state overwrite via hash collision) requires exploiting the execution layer.

phase3.summary: The invariant (keccak256 collision resistance for Ethereum address/storage key hashing) is vacuously true in this codebase because keccak256 is not used for this purpose. For actual keccak256 usages, golang.org/x/crypto/sha3 LegacyKeccak256 is a standards-conformant implementation with no known collisions. Hash output is not truncated before use in either actual usage site.
phase3.guard_identified: sha3.NewLegacyKeccak256 from golang.org/x/crypto — standards-conformant implementation; output used at full 32-byte length in all actual usages
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient for actual usages in this codebase. The property's stated scenario (EVM trie collision) is not a concern for Prysm.
edge_cases: crypto/keystore/keccak256.go returns []byte — callers in keystore.go use it for MAC comparison. MAC comparison should be constant-time to prevent timing side channels. This is an informational note, not related to the trie collision property being audited.

phase3_5.reason: The property (keccak256 collision resistance for EVM address/storage key hashing) does not apply to Prysm, which is a consensus client that does not perform EVM address or storage key hashing. The resolved code location is incorrect (grep_fallback mismatch). The actual keccak256 usage in this codebase (deposit event signature, keystore MAC) does not involve the collision scenario described.
phase3_5.recommendation: Re-target to execution client code (go-ethereum trie package or similar). Informational: verify keystore MAC comparison uses constant-time comparison to prevent timing side channels (unrelated to this property).
